source.title: Optimal Transport Model Distributional Robustness
source.authors: Van-Anh Nguyen; Trung Le; A. Bui; Thanh-Toan Do; Dinh Q. Phung

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices; no relevant truncation is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study develops OT-MDR as a sharpness-aware training method and compares it with SAM and other baselines. It reports natural-label accuracy and qualitative loss landscapes, but does not test any of the claim versions’ specified interventions or measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports accuracy and uncertainty metrics for OT-MDR and baselines, plus qualitative loss-landscape comparisons. These do not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected networks, optimizer or batch-size effects, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. The loss-landscape results are not the magnitude-aware perturbation measure in V7.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flat-minima rationale to develop OT-MDR and evaluates its accuracy and uncertainty estimates. It does not test any specified version. Figure 2 shows qualitative loss landscapes, without magnitude-aware sharpness, measured generalization gaps, or comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures required by V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors present OT-MDR as a probabilistic extension of SAM, recover SAM as a special case, and report improvements in single-model, ensemble, and Bayesian settings. Their broader claim of improvement across all metrics overstates Table 4: CIFAR-10 ResNet10 NLL and ECE are numerically worse with OT-MDR.
record.recipe_differences: OT-MDR uses two perturbed models per particle and random mini-batch splits; the authors compare it with SAM and other methods. It is trained on natural-label CIFAR data with data augmentation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported ablation says accuracy is higher with two particles than one, then worsens as particle count increases; the authors describe diminishing returns and possible performance deterioration. Figure 1 gives no exact accuracies in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: OT-MDR has higher reported test accuracy than SAM in all six Table 1 comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: One-particle OT-MDR improves CIFAR accuracy over SAM for the three tested architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: OT-MDR has higher reported ResNet18 accuracy than the SGD, SAM, and bSAM results borrowed from reference 48.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: OT-MDR exceeds the listed published ResNet18 CIFAR accuracy baselines under the adopted evaluation setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2 qualitatively depicts lower, flatter ensemble loss regions for OT-MDR than SAM on CIFAR-100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: OT-MDR produces qualitatively flatter ensemble loss landscapes than SAM in the illustrated comparisons.

record.problems: The study does not report training accuracy or train-test gaps for these comparisons. It says Table 2 baseline results are taken from another paper. The multi-particle ablation is reported as a figure without exact values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Rows from Tables 3 and 4, including ensemble and BNN metrics, are omitted because they report other OT-MDR benchmark comparisons rather than a condition or measure specified by the claim versions; the selected rows preserve the directly tabulated single-model accuracy comparisons.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the comparison of natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and local-connectivity interventions.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning. Using SGD for single models and Adam for BNNs does not isolate optimizer effects.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove a large-batch penalty. Splitting batches within OT-MDR does not test this.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with measured train-test gaps at similarly low training loss, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: No version-specific verdict is warranted. The ± values in Table 1 accompany three random-seed runs, but their statistical definition is unspecified. The text's claimed average Table 1 improvements do not match the tabulated differences: these average approximately 0.31 percentage points on CIFAR-10 and 1.39 on CIFAR-100.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and the stated local-connectivity conditions.
Comparisons isolating adaptive optimizers from SGD under the stated tuning regimes.
Large versus small batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions and the stated training-set-size or augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurement and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing the most memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
